 Judgment

This appeal under Section 374(2) of Cr.P.C. is filed by the accused/appellant with a prayer to set aside the judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by the Court of Sessions Judge,
Yadgiri in Sessions Case No.52/2014 dated 20.06.2018, wherein, the appellant has been convicted for the offence punishable under Section 376 of IPC and sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of ten years and pay fine of Rs.50,000/- and in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of six months.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.

3. Brief facts of the case leading to filing of this appeal as revealed from the records are - The FIR in Crime No.51/2014 was registered by Shorapur police station, Yadgiri against the appellant for the offences punishable under Sections 376 and 506 of IPC NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 on the basis of the first information dated 08.03.2014 received from the victim - PW.4.
The police after investigation filed charge sheet against the appellant for the aforesaid offences.
The charges that were framed by the Trial Court were read over and explained to the appellant and since he denied the same and claimed to be tried.
The prosecution in order to prove its charges against the appellant totally examined 17 witnesses as PW.1 to PW.17 and 17 documents were marked as Exs.P1 to P17.

Four material objects were marked as MO.1 to MO.4.
4.
After evidence of the prosecution was closed, the statement of the accused was recorded under Section 313 of Cr.P.C., however, no defence evidence was led on behalf of the accused.

The Trial Court after hearing the arguments on both sides, acquitted the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 506 of IPC and convicted him for the offence punishable under Section 376 of IPC and sentenced him to undergo simple imprisonment for a NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 period of 10 years and pay fine of `50,000/- and in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months.
Being aggrieved by the same, the appellant is before this Court.

Basangouda vs The State on 14 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37289732/
2 5.
Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the Trial Court was not justified in basing the conviction on the sole testimony of PW.4 - victim, when the statements made by her are not consistent.
He submits that PW.2 - Tammanna, who according to the victim had rescued her has not supported the case of the prosecution.
He submits that there a delay in lodging the FIR and there is no explanation for the same.
He also submits that the medical records do not support the case of the prosecution.

The evidence of PW.4 - victim appears to be unnatural and therefore, based on her sole testimony the Trial Court should not have convicted the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 376 of IPC.
Accordingly, he prays to allow the appeal.

Per contra, learned High Court Government Pleader, who has opposed the prayer made in the appeal memorandum submits that the victim after informing her husband about the alleged incident had approached the police station and therefore, there is a delay in registering the FIR.

He submits that PW.4 - victim has clearly stated that the appellant had forcibly intercourse with her against her wish in his flourmill on 06.03.2014 and there is no reason to disbelieve her statement.

For offence punishable under Section 376 of IPC, the sole testimony of the victim is sufficient to convict the appellant/accused and therefore no illegality or irregularity can be found in the judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the Trial Court.
Accordingly, he prays to dismiss the appeal.
7. The prosecution in order to prove the charges against the appellant/accused, in all examined 17 witnesses before the Trial Court as PW.1 to PW.17.
PW.1 is the Head Constable who carried the FIR to the jurisdictional Court of Magistrate.
PW.2-Tammanna is the NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 person who is said to have rescued the victim-lady immediately after the alleged act of sexual assault was committed by the appellant.
PW.3 is the pancha to the mahazar Ex.P.3 and PW.4 is the victim.
PW.5 is another pancha to mahazar Ex.P.3 and PW.6 is the father of the appellant/accused.
PW.7 and PW.8 are the independent witnesses who were examined by the prosecution.
PW.9 is the Panchayat Secretary and PW.10 is the Doctor who has medically examined the victim - lady.
PW.11 is the husband of the victim -lady and PW.12 is the Junior Engineer of PWD who had prepared the sketch of the spot.

PW.13 is the Doctor who has medically examined the appellant and PW.14 is the pancha to the recovery mahazar, PW.15 is also another pancha to the recovery mahazar and PW.16 is the Assistant Engineer of GESCOM who has issued certificate as per Ex.P.16.
PW.17 is the Inspector of Police who has investigated the case and filed the charge-sheet.
All the independent witnesses except the victim-lady and her husband have turned hostile to the case of the prosecution.

PW.4/victim-lady in her first information had stated that on 06.03.2014 she had gone to the flourmill of the appellant herein at about 8.00 p.m. and when she was in the flourmill, there was a power cut and taking advantage of the darkness inside the flourmill, the appellant pulled her inside the flourmill and after bolting the door, committed the act of sexual assault on her against her wish.
She has further stated that PW.2- Tammanna who resides near the flourmill heard her cry and opened the door and rescued her.

If the allegation against the appellant that he had bolted the door Basangouda vs The State on 14 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37289732/
3 lock from inside and committed sexual assault on the victim is correct, then it becomes highly doubtful as to how Tammanna would have unlocked the door from outside.

sentences.text:
In addition to the same,
Tammanna who is examined as PW.2 has not supported the case of the prosecution.
The sketch of the spot of crime does not reflect that Tammanna's residence is situated near the flourmill of the appellant.
On the other hand, house of Lingappa Poojari is situated next to the flourmill of the appellant.
Said NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 Lingappa Poojari has not been examined in the present case.

9. The statement of the victim-lady under Section 164 of Cr.P.C was recorded before the jurisdictional Magistrate and in her said statement, she has stated that after the appellant had committed sexual assault on her, his father Shekappa (PW.6) had locked the door of the flourmill from outside and thereafter Tammanna opened the door and had sent her home.

There is lot of discrepancy in the statement of the victim- lady made in her complaint Ex.P.1 and in her statement given before the Magistrate under Section 164 of Cr.P.C. Shekappa who is examined as PW.6 in the present case also has not supported the case of the prosecution.
10. The victim-lady/PW.4 has stated that the incident had taken place at about 8.00 p.m. on 06.03.2014 and after the incident had taken place she had gone to her home.
She has also stated that her husband was not in station and he had returned home on NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 07.03.2014 and on the said day she had informed him about the incident.
However the first information was lodged before the police on 08.03.2014 at about 1.00 a.m.
PW.11 is the husband of the victim-lady (PW.4).

During the course of his deposition he has stated that he had returned home on the date of the incident itself and on the very same day PW.4 had informed him about the alleged act of sexual assault committed by the appellant.

If that is so, there is inordinate delay in approaching the police which is not explained properly either by PW.4 or by PW.11 and therefore a serious doubt arises with regard to the correctness of the allegations made against the appellant.
11. PW.10 is the Doctor who has medically examined the victim lady.
She has clearly stated that no signs of forcible sex were found on the body of the victim- lady when the victim-lady was examined by her on 08.03.2024.

PW.4 during the course of her deposition has stated that she has not suffered any injuries on her body - 10 - NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 when the appellant had sexually assaulted her inside the flourmill against her wishes.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Manak Chand @ Mani vs. State of Haryana1 in paragraph 5 has observed as follows :-
"5.

entities.text: Manak Chand @ Mani vs. State of Haryana1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The evidence of a prosecutrix in a case of rape is of the same value as that of an injured witness.
It is again true that conviction can be made on the basis of the sole testimony of the prosecutrix.

All the same, when a conviction can be based on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix, the courts also have to be extremely careful while examining this sole testimony as cautioned in State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh, (1996)
2 SCC 384:
Basangouda vs The State on 14 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37289732/
4

entities.text:
State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh, (1996)
2 SCC 384
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "If evidence of the prosecutrix inspires confidence, it must be relied upon without seeking corroboration of her statement in material particulars.

If for some reason the court finds it difficult to place implicit reliance on her testimony, it may look for evidence which may lend assurance to her testimony, short of corroboration required in the case of an accomplice.

The testimony of the prosecutrix must be appreciated in the background of the entire case and the trial court must be alive to its responsibility and be sensitive while dealing with cases involving sexual molestations."

This was reiterated by this Court in Sadashiv Ramrao Hadbe v. State of Maharashtra and Another (2006) 10 SCC 92:
[2024] ACR 66 - 11 - NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 "It is true that in a rape case the accused could be convicted on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix, if it is capable of inspiring confidence in the mind of the court.

entities.text: Sadashiv Ramrao Hadbe v. State of Maharashtra and Another (2006) 10 SCC 92
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If the version given by the prosecutrix is unsupported by any medical evidence or the whole surrounding circumstances are highly improbable and belie the case set up by the prosecutrix, the court shall not act on the solitary evidence of the prosecutrix."

Both the prosecutrix as well as the accused have a right for a fair trial, and therefore when the statement of the prosecutrix does not inspire confidence and creates a doubt, the court must look for corroborative evidence.

Relying upon the case of Gurmit Singh (supra) this court in Raju and others v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2008) 15 SCC 133 held as under:
"10.

entities.text: Raju and others v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2008) 15 SCC 133
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The aforesaid judgments lay down the basic principle that ordinarily the evidence of a prosecutrix should not be suspected and should be believed, more so as her statement has to be evaluated on a par with that of an injured witness and if the evidence is reliable, no corroboration is necessary.

Undoubtedly, the aforesaid observations must carry the greatest weight and we respectfully agree with them, but at the same time they cannot be universally and mechanically applied to the facts of every case of sexual assault which comes before the court.

11. It cannot be lost sight of that rape causes the greatest distress and humiliation to the victim but at the same time a false allegation of rape can cause equal distress,
humiliation and damage to the accused as well.
The accused must also be protected against the possibility of false implication, particularly where a large number of accused are involved.

It must, further, be borne in - 12 - Basangouda vs The State on 14 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/37289732/
5 NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 mind that the broad principle is that an injured witness was present at the time when the incident happened and that ordinarily such a witness would not tell a lie as to the actual assailants, but there is no presumption or any basis for assuming that the statement of such a witness is always correct or without any embellishment or exaggeration.""
12.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the present case, the Trial Court has passed the order of conviction solely on the basis of the testimony of victim-lady (PW.4) and considering the discrepancies in the evidence of PW.4 and also in the background of the delay in lodging the FIR, I am of the considered opinion that it is not safe to convict the appellant only on the basis of the sole testimony of the victim-lady which does not inspire confidence in the mind of the Court.

The initial statement of the victim-lady that PW.14 - Tammanna had opened the door and rescued her from the flourmill and her subsequent statement under Section 164 of Cr.P.C before the Magistrate that father of the appellant had locked the door from outside after the appellant had committed the act of sexual assault on her and it was Tammanna (PW.2) who thereafter came and rescued her - 13 - NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 etc., rises a serious doubt about the correctness of the allegation made against the appellant.

In addition to the same, PW.2-Tammanna and PW.6-Shekappagouda have not supported the case of the prosecution and though they were cross-examined by the prosecution nothing material has been elicited from their mouth.
Therefore, I am of the considered opinion that the Trial Court was not justified in convicting the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 376 of IPC.

Accordingly, the following :
ORDER
The criminal appeal is allowed.

The judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the Court of Sessions Judge, Yadgiri in S.C.No.52/2014 dated 20.06.2018 convicting the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 376 of ICP is set- aside.

Bail bonds, if any of the appellant stands cancelled.
- 14 - NC: 2024:KHC-K:3900 Fine amount, if any, deposited by the appellant is refunded to the same.
